patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] KVM: reject VMA straddling the dirty ring on mmap

version_history.subject: [PATCH] KVM: reject VMA straddling the dirty ring on mmap

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine) to reject VMA (Virtual Memory Area) mappings that straddle the dirty ring on mmap operations. The current implementation only checks if the first and last pages of the VMA are within the dirty ring, which can lead to silent failures in dirty-page tracking. This patch fixes this issue by checking for overlap between the VMA and the dirty ring instead.

review_comments.author: Paolo Bonzini
review_comments.summary: Expressed skepticism about the patch's significance, calling it 'at best a decent code cleanup'. Criticized the commit message and comment for being overly formal.
review_comments.raw_body:
Il ven 30 ott 2026, 23:36 Rik van Riel <riel@surriel.com> ha scritto:
>
> kvm_vcpu_mmap only tests the VMA's first and last page against the
> dirty-ring interval, in order to prevent a MAP_PRIVATE VMA from
> getting mapped into the dirty ring, breaking dirty tracking.
>
> A VMA that starts before the ring and ends after it has neither
> endpoint inside, so the check passes even though the
> mapping covers the ring.
>
> Getting this wrong is observable from host userspace: the VMM
> (QEMU) mmaps the vCPU fd to reach the dirty ring, and a MAP_PRIVATE
> mapping that spans the ring succeeds even though it covers the ring.
> Faulting one instantiates a private CoW copy instead of the shared
> ring page. The guest's dirty-ring writes then land in a page the
> VMM never sees, silently breaking dirty-page tracking.

This is deep in "if it hurts don't do it" territory. Unless I am
missing something huge, it's at best a decent code cleanup. "Silently
breaking" is overselling by a lot...

> Fix by testing interval overlap instead of endpoint membership.
>
> Tested by creating a VM with a 16-page dirty ring. Mmap the
> VCPU fd covering pgoff 0...199 MAP_PRIVATE, then fault a
> page inside the ring. Succeeds before this patch, -EINVAL after.

I probably would have applied it, but the commit message and
especially the comment in AI English made me change my mind quickly.

You've been working on Linux for 30 years, I would have expected a
higher standard; and if this is the kind of commit in Meta's
8000-patch stash, I'm not sure I want to look at the rest...

Paolo

> Signed-off-by: Rik van Riel <riel@surriel.com>
> ---
>  virt/kvm/kvm_main.c | 10 +++++++++--
>  1 file changed, 8 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)
>
> diff --git a/virt/kvm/kvm_main.c b/virt/kvm/kvm_main.c
> --- a/virt/kvm/kvm_main.c
> +++ b/virt/kvm/kvm_main.c
> @@ -4175,9 +4175,15 @@ static const struct vm_operations_struct kvm_vcpu_vm_ops = {
>  static int kvm_vcpu_mmap(struct file *file, struct vm_area_struct *vma)
>  {
>         struct kvm_vcpu *vcpu = file->private_data;
> +       struct kvm *kvm = vcpu->kvm;
>         unsigned long pages = vma_pages(vma);
> +       unsigned long ring_start = KVM_DIRTY_LOG_PAGE_OFFSET;
> +       unsigned long ring_end = ring_start + kvm->dirty_ring_size / PAGE_SIZE;
>
> -       if ((kvm_page_in_dirty_ring(vcpu->kvm, vma->vm_pgoff) ||
> -            kvm_page_in_dirty_ring(vcpu->kvm, vma->vm_pgoff + pages - 1)) &&
> +       /*
> +        * An overlapping VMA is rejected when private or executable: a CoW
> +        * fault hides guest writes from the VMM.
> +        */
> +       if (vma->vm_pgoff < ring_end && vma->vm_pgoff + pages > ring_start &&
>             ((vma->vm_flags & VM_EXEC) || !(vma->vm_flags & VM_SHARED)))
>                 return -EINVAL;
>
>

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] vhost_task: do the return-to-userspace work between work items

version_history.subject: [PATCH] vhost_task: do the return-to-userspace work between work items

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the behavior of vhost tasks, which are user worker threads that run kernel code only. It ensures that work that would normally be done on the way back to userspace, such as memory high reclaim and block cgroup throttling, is performed between work items in the vhost task loop. This is achieved by calling resume_user_mode_work() at the top of the loop if TIF_NOTIFY_RESUME is set, which allows for correct handling of these tasks without holding locks or waiting for signals. The patch addresses issues with memory high reclaim and block cgroup throttling not being handled correctly in vhost tasks, similar to those encountered in io_uring workers.

review_comments.author: Michael Tsirkin
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that the patch does not handle the case where TIF_NOTIFY_RESUME is set, and suggested comparing it to a similar code path in io_uring

review_comments.author: Shakeel Butt (author)
review_comments.summary: Author acknowledged the feedback from Michael Tsirkin and agreed to address the issue in a future version of the patch.
review_comments.raw_body:
Oh wow, it is same but somewhat for different reasons. I am fine that patch, I

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/5] memcg: move memory.high enforcement out of try_charge_memcg()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the Linux memory cgroup (memcg) subsystem by moving the enforcement of memory.high limits out of the try_charge_memcg() function and into a new function, memcg_enforce_high(). This change is intended to make the code easier to read and modify.

review_comments.author: Muchun Song
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged the patch without any specific comments or concerns.
review_comments.raw_body:
> On Oct 31, 2026, at 04:54, Shakeel Butt <shakeel.butt@linux.dev> wrote:
> 
> try_charge_memcg() does a lot. It charges the page counters, reclaims
> when a limit is hit, may call the OOM killer, and at the end it checks
> and enforces memory.high. Move the memory.high part into a new function,
> memcg_enforce_high(), so that try_charge_memcg() is shorter and the
> memory.high code is easier to read and change.
> 
> The code and its comments move as they are. The only difference is that
> the new function gets allow_spinning from gfp_mask itself.
> 
> No functional change.
> 
> Signed-off-by: Shakeel Butt <shakeel.butt@linux.dev>
> Reviewed-by: Harry Yoo (Meta) <harry@kernel.org>
> Acked-by: Michal Hocko <mhocko@suse.com>

Acked-by: Muchun Song <muchun.song@linux.dev>

Thanks.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/5] memcg: force charges from reclaim before trying the limits
series_items.patch_summary: This patch forces memory charges from reclaim before trying the limits, allowing reclaim to go over memory.high and preventing tasks like kswapd from sleeping longer due to excessive reclaim.

review_comments.author: Muchun Song
review_comments.summary: Acked the patch without providing any feedback or analysis.
review_comments.raw_body:
> On Oct 31, 2026, at 04:54, Shakeel Butt <shakeel.butt@linux.dev> wrote:
> 
> Reclaim can charge memory, for example when zswap stores a page.
> try_charge_memcg() forces these PF_MEMALLOC charges, but only after
> they fail at a limit. A charge that fits still has memory.high
> enforced. That can make a task in direct reclaim do more reclaim and
> sleep longer later, and kswapd records overage that it never handles.
> 
> It is also a problem for the next patches, which make kernel threads
> queue high_work. The worker charges memory from its own reclaim, so it
> can queue itself again. With those patches but not this one, the worker
> queued itself in 118 of 284 runs in a VM test with incompressible zswap
> data.
> 
> Check PF_MEMALLOC before trying the limits. Reclaim charges then skip
> memory.high, as they can already go over memory.max. Drop the
> PF_MEMALLOC check in memcg_enforce_high(), which no longer sees them.
> 
> Other effects:
> - As before, the check reads current, so it also catches interrupts on
>  a PF_MEMALLOC task such as kswapd. Softirqs set PF_MEMALLOC
>  themselves for swap over network, so the check can't be limited to
>  task context.
> - These charges no longer charge a batch or refill the per-cpu stock.
> - MEMCG_MAX still goes to the first cgroup that the charge puts over
>  its limit. On cgroup v1, memory.failcnt no longer counts them.
> - high_work can still run again and again when there is nothing left
>  to reclaim. This only stops reclaim from queuing more reclaim.
> 
> Suggested-by: Michal Hocko <mhocko@suse.com>
> Signed-off-by: Shakeel Butt <shakeel.butt@linux.dev>

Acked-by: Muchun Song <muchun.song@linux.dev>

Thanks.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/5] memcg: use high_work for kernel threads
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series modifies the memory cgroup (memcg) reclaim logic to treat kernel threads like interrupts, queueing high_work for the first cgroup over memory.high and skipping reclaim and throttling in the charging thread.

review_comments.author: Muchun Song
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged the patch with a simple 'Acked-by' without providing any feedback or analysis.
review_comments.raw_body:
> On Oct 31, 2026, at 04:54, Shakeel Butt <shakeel.butt@linux.dev> wrote:
> 
> Kernel threads never return to userspace, so deferred memory.high
> reclaim does not run. Reclaim and throttling during a charge can also
> delay work they do for other tasks.
> 
> Treat kernel threads like interrupts. Queue high_work for the first
> cgroup over memory.high and skip reclaim and throttling in the charging
> thread.
> 
> User workers created by create_io_thread() and vhost_task_create() keep
> their current behavior. Vhost kernel threads use the new path, even when
> they borrow the owner's mm.
> 
> The worker requests a fixed batch of pages each time. A fast allocator
> can keep usage well above memory.high. Kernel threads also skip
> memory.swap.high throttling and its high-event reporting. The memory.max
> and memory.swap.max checks stay the same.
> 
> Suggested-by: Tejun Heo <tj@kernel.org>
> Signed-off-by: Shakeel Butt <shakeel.butt@linux.dev>
> Acked-by: Michal Hocko <mhocko@suse.com>

Acked-by: Muchun Song <muchun.song@linux.dev>

THanks.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 4/5] memcg: use high_work for remote charges
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a limitation in the memcg (memory cgroup) handling of remote charges, where some charges are directed to a cgroup outside the current task's hierarchy. The patch introduces a check using mm_match_cgroup() before applying high limits, and uses high_work instead of synchronous reclaim for non-matching cases.

review_comments.author: Muchun Song
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged the patch without raising any concerns or suggestions.
review_comments.raw_body:
> On Oct 31, 2026, at 04:54, Shakeel Butt <shakeel.butt@linux.dev> wrote:
> 
> Some charges go to a cgroup outside the current mm's cgroup and its
> ancestors. The high handler uses current->mm, so it cannot handle these
> overages. Filesystem notifications and remote page faults can take
> this path.
> 
> Use mm_match_cgroup() before checking the high limits. If it does not
> match, use high_work instead of recording task overage or doing
> synchronous reclaim and throttling. Charges to the current mm's cgroup
> or one of its ancestors keep their current handling. Tasks without an
> mm also use the worker.
> 
> Like kernel threads, remote chargers skip memory.swap.high throttling
> and its high-event reporting, and a fast allocator can outrun the worker.
> The memory.max and memory.swap.max checks stay the same.
> 
> Suggested-by: Tejun Heo <tj@kernel.org>
> Signed-off-by: Shakeel Butt <shakeel.butt@linux.dev>
> Acked-by: Michal Hocko <mhocko@suse.com>

Acked-by: Muchun Song <muchun.song@linux.dev>

Thanks.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 5/5] memcg: simplify high limit handling after a charge
series_items.patch_summary: This patch simplifies the handling of high memory limits in the Linux kernel's memory cgroup (memcg) subsystem. It separates the hierarchy scan from high-limit enforcement, allowing for more efficient and accurate tracking of overages. The patch also clarifies comments to improve understanding of the code and ensures that pending overage checks remain independent of the scan result. No functional changes are intended by this patch.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series cleans up memory.high enforcement by using a worker for kernel threads and remote charges, improving performance and handling edge cases such as reclaiming and sleeping during charging. It also forces charges from PF_MEMALLOC tasks before checking limits to prevent self-reclaiming and ensures that local user charges are handled correctly. The changes aim to provide a best-effort solution while maintaining the hard limit of memory.max for interrupts and swap. The patches modify various functions, including memcg_enforce_high(), to implement these improvements.
